title: Like stars, like dew (section 32)
hook: look on the world like stars, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud (Müller, section 32)

segments.voice: Yesterday, views of self: what the Tathagata taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and so it's called a view. Your line: so-called views. Which opinion did you hold a little more loosely? Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

Dew covers the car in the driveway at six in the morning. Every inch of the windshield is beaded and silver. By the time the coffee's poured, the sun is over the fence, and by the time the keys are found, the glass is dry. Nobody saw it leave. The Diamond Sutra has spent weeks cutting: self, marks, merit, views. Now, in its last section, it stops cutting and does something no blade does. It hands over a few pictures, plain enough for a child, and says: look at the world like this. Today: like stars.
screen: `DEW ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `DRY BEFORE THE KEYS ARE FOUND.` → `THE BLADE HANDS OVER PICTURES.`

segments.voice: First, one last comparison. Suppose someone filled worlds beyond measure with jewels and gave them all away. And suppose someone else took even four lines of this teaching, kept them, and explained them to others. The second, the Buddha says, makes the greater merit. And how should it be explained? In the sutra's own way, paraphrased: without taking hold of the explaining, so that it's only called explaining. Second, the verse. Then the Buddha gives a short verse, and in paraphrase it says: look on all that is made like stars, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud. Each picture is something you can actually see. Stars, which shine all night and fade at dawn. A lamp, which burns only while the oil lasts. A magician's illusion. Dew, gone before the keys are found. A bubble. A dream that felt like a whole life. A flash of lightning. A cloud, changing shape as you watch. Third, what the verse does not say. It doesn't say the world is fake. Dew is really dew; it really wets the glass. A few days ago the sutra warned against hearing emptiness as nothing. The verse holds both: real, and passing; here, and not fixed. Fourth, the ending. The Buddha finishes. And the elder Subhuti, the monks and nuns, the lay men and women, gods and humans and other beings, the sutra says, all rejoice at what the Buddha has said. The Diamond Sutra began with an ordinary morning: a bowl, a meal, washed feet. It ends with a lamp, a bubble, and a crowd that is glad.
screen: `FOUR LINES OUTWEIGH THE JEWELS.` · `STARS, A LAMP, DEW, A BUBBLE.` · `REAL, AND PASSING.` · `THE ASSEMBLY REJOICES.` · then, large: `LIKE DEW, LIKE LIGHTNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: watch dew or a bubble. If there's a glass of something fizzy nearby, watch the bubbles rise and break. If there's a window, look for any drop of water, or the breath fogging the glass and fading. If neither, close your eyes and watch the breath itself: it forms, it fills, it's gone. Let one picture from the verse sit with you, stars or dew or lightning. Notice the thing is real while it lasts, and notice it doesn't last. Hold both, gently. The bell holds the time.
Like stars. The opening picture of the Diamond Sutra's closing verse: look on all that is made like stars, a lamp, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud. Today's word.
Your line: like dew, like lightning. Today, when something good or hard is happening, say quietly: like dew. Then enjoy it, or bear it, while it lasts. Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Mahayana communities recite the closing verse of the Diamond Sutra on its own, at the end of chanting the sutra and at other times, as a short reminder that all that is made is passing.

fork.setup: the sutra is ending. you're asked how to explain its four lines to someone else. what does section 32 say?
options: explain them as the final truth
explain them without taking hold of the explaining
fork.reveal: the sutra says explain them, but in its own way: without clutching, so it's only called explaining. then comes the verse.

original.note: Sanskrit: a star; the first picture in the Diamond Sutra's closing verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says nothing in the world is real.
what it means: all that is made is like dew or lightning: really here, and not lasting.
what a scholar hears: the verse is about the 'made' or conditioned world, and it closes the sutra just before the assembly rejoices.

notes: The closing verse is paraphrased, not quoted: the outline cites Max Müller's rendering, but his exact wording was not verified. A Keeper may wish to supply Müller's text verbatim.

The Sanskrit verse has one more image than the outline lists (often rendered darkness, or a fault of vision, after the stars), and Kumarajiva's Chinese version gives a different, shorter list; the script follows the outline's images and makes no count. Confirm.
'Explain without taking hold of the explaining, so it's only called explaining' paraphrases the Sanskrit 'as one who would not illuminate; therefore it is called illuminating'; confirm.
Original-language word: taraka as the verse's 'stars'; confirm spelling and pronunciation.
Day 1149 closes Block C (the Diamond Sutra); the teach's final lines look back to section 1.
Editor: varied the hook opening, which mirrored day 1147's 'Late afternoon, and the light'; 'gone at dawn' became 'fade at dawn' for the stars; softened the howItsDone recitation claim.
